title: What to Know About the Threat of a ‘Dirty Bomb’ Amid Reported Iran Plot
author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
body:
Iran is reportedly developing potential plans to detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington, D.C., a threat that one member of the House Intelligence Committee called an intimidation tactic.

Citing seven U.S. officials, CNN reported on Monday that new U.S. intelligence indicates planning by Iran to target Trump Administration officials in an attack on the capital. Intelligence reportedly also intercepted Iranian chatter claiming to have stashed bomb-making materials inside the U.S., although officials disagree about the credibility of that claim.

Such an attack would be a major escalation. Since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran on Feb. 28, Iran has attacked U.S. military bases in the Middle East, as well as energy facilities, commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, and U.S. allies in the Gulf. But it has not launched a direct attack on American soil. U.S. officials reportedly see the intelligence as a sign that Iran may be eyeing escalation amid stalled negotiations.

But U.S. officials said intelligence does not necessarily indicate an imminent threat, and they are still assessing whether Iran could or would carry out such an attack.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to CNN that the U.S. is “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.” TIME has reached out to the White House and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which the Defense Department referred to, for comment.

Representative André Carson (D, Ind.) told CNN on Monday that the House Intelligence Committee gets “these kinds of reports quite often,” but many do not become public.

An official told CNN that Iran is cognizant of the risk of retaliation if it were to attack the U.S.

Nevertheless, the report raises questions about U.S. preparedness against an attack using an unconventional weapon. It would be “extremely easy,” one official reportedly said, for operatives to have entered the U.S. over the past decade and pre-positioned bomb components or nuclear materials within the country.

Officials have reportedly discussed countermeasures against the potential threat in Washington, and contingency planning against threats in the Middle East.

Attorney General Todd Blanche last week urged congressional leaders to reauthorize a national security law that allows U.S. authorities to surveil foreign nationals abroad. Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act expired in June, although existing surveillance orders remain valid until March 2027.

The New York Times reported on Nov. 3 that Israel had shared intelligence suggesting Iran was considering using chemical weapons against its adversaries, an assessment that divided U.S. officials. Officials told CNN that American troops in the Middle East would not have adequate protection or training in the event of such an attack.

A spokesperson for the Iranian Mission at the United Nations in New York rejected the allegations of chemical weapons planning. Iran “considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be wholly illegitimate and categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations circulated in this regard,” the spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.

What is a ‘dirty bomb’?

A dirty bomb is a weapon that combines a conventional explosive, like dynamite or TNT, with radioactive material. It is not a nuclear weapon and its explosion is millions of times less powerful than an atomic bomb. While a detonated nuclear weapon spreads radiation across thousands of square miles, a dirty bomb could scatter radioactive debris over a few blocks or miles.

It takes relatively little expertise to build a dirty bomb, according to the Council on Foreign Relations. “No special assembly is required; the regular explosive simply disperses the radioactive material packed into the bomb,” CFR writes. “The hardest part is acquiring the radioactive material, not building the bomb.”

But CFR notes that not all dirty bombs are equally dangerous. How much damage it can do depends on access to sophisticated technologies needed to handle highly radioactive material.

Most of the danger from a dirty bomb comes from the initial explosion, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The radioactive materials scattered by a dirty bomb are unlikely to produce enough radiation exposure to cause immediate serious illness, except to those very close to the blast site, the CDC says.

But the radioactive dust and smoke can still be dangerous if inhaled, and the CDC recommends covering your nose and mouth with a cloth if you are outside or in a car near the explosion site, and entering a nearby building where the walls and windows have not been broken. Avoid touching any objects thrown off by the explosion, and once you are indoors, shut all windows, remove and seal your outer layer of clothing in a plastic bag, and shower with soap and water.

Experts sometimes point to the radiological accident in Goiânia, Brazil, in 1987 as an illustration of the potential consequences of radioactive contamination. On Sept. 13, 1987, scavengers broke into an abandoned private radiotherapy clinic and removed part of a teletherapy machine containing a cesium-137 source. The capsule was punctured days later, exposing cesium chloride that emitted a blue glow. Unaware of the danger, people rubbed the powder on their skin and shared it with others over two weeks. Four people died from radiation exposure. More than 100,000 people were screened after the hazard was identified, and 249 were found to have radioactive contamination. Authorities oversaw extensive environmental remediation, including the demolition of multiple homes.

Has a dirty bomb been used before?

Never has a dirty bomb been detonated in an attack before, although there have been several attempts and plots to use one. Iraq tested a one-ton radiological bomb in 1987, according to CFR, but found that the radiation levels it generated were too weak to make the weapon effective.

In what a chronology compiled by PBS describes as “the first-ever attempt at radiological terror,” Chechen rebels in November 1995 told a Russian TV station that they planted a cache of radioactive material in Moscow’s Izmailovsky Park. A TV crew located a partially buried container holding cesium-137 in the park. Authorities removed the container and no explosion occurred.

In 2002, the U.S. arrested Jose Padilla, an American citizen and alleged al-Qaeda operative, on suspicion of plotting to build and detonate a dirty bomb in a U.S. city. Padilla was arrested in Chicago after he returned from Pakistan, and designated an enemy combatant. He was held in military custody for more than three years without formal criminal charges. The government omitted the “dirty bomb” allegations from his 2005 indictment in civilian court, but he was convicted in 2007 of terrorism-related offences. He was released on Nov. 12 after serving nearly 21 years in prison after his indictment.

In October 2022, eight months after invading Ukraine, Russian officials accused Ukraine of preparing to detonate a dirty bomb in what they said would be a false-flag attack to blame Moscow. Ukraine rejected the allegations, and Western officials warned that Russia would use the claims as a pretext for an escalation. Ukraine formally requested an inspection by the International Atomic Energy Agency, which found no sign of undeclared nuclear activity or materials at three locations inspected.

Previous Iranian threats to the U.S.

The reported planning suggests Iran is considering expanding its methods to include radiological or chemical attacks, but it’s not the first time Iran has planned or attempted an attack within the U.S.

U.S. prosecutors have charged members and associates of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in multiple alleged plots to assassinate people on American soil. U.S. intelligence has also flagged other suspected Iranian plans for attacks.

Prosecutors have brought multiple cases since the war began more than eight months ago. On Nov. 10, federal prosecutors in Manhattan announced an expanded indictment against three men—Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani—accused of orchestrating attacks for groups linked to the IRGC and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kata’ib Hizballah. The allegations include 18 attacks and attempted attacks in Europe, a plot to bomb a Manhattan synagogue, and a September plot against a British air base housing U.S. personnel.

Last week, the Secret Service reportedly moved Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into military housing because of threats to his life that were linked to Iran. Bessent has led the Trump Administration’s sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran that has crippled the country’s economy alongside a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports.

In February, an FBI bulletin circulated, suggesting that Iran was considering launching drones from a vessel offshore against targets in California if the U.S. attacked Iran. No such attack followed the U.S. strikes, and the White House later said the warning rested on a single unverified tip.

Iranian state media have also circulated threats against President Donald Trump and his family.

In 2024, U.S. authorities also accused Iran of two assassination plots targeting Trump. In one, Pakistani national Asif Merchant sought to hire undercover officers posing as hitmen to kill Trump. He was convicted in March. In the other, prosecutors alleged that an IRGC official instructed Afghan national Farhad Shakeri in October 2024 to develop a plan to kill Trump. Neither plot resulted in an attack.

Iran has been linked to several other assassinations and plots in the U.S. In July 1980, Iranian dissident and former diplomat Ali Akbar Tabatabai was murdered at his home in Bethesda, Md. Dawud Salahuddin later admitted to killing him at the behest of the Iranian government.

In 2011, U.S. authorities disrupted a plot to assassinate Saudi Ambassador Adel al-Jubeir by bombing a restaurant in Washington, D.C. Manssor Arbabsiar pleaded guilty to conspiring with Iranian Quds Force officials to kill the ambassador, and was sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2013.

In 2021, IRGC member Shahram Poursafi allegedly offered $300,000 to arrange the murder of former national security adviser John Bolton in Washington or Maryland, in apparent retaliation for the U.S. killing of Iranian General Qassem Soleimani. And in 2023, the Justice Department charged two men allegedly linked to the IRGC with a murder-for-hire plot against Masih Alinejad, an Iranian-American journalist and critic of Iran’s government. Two organizers were convicted in March 2025 for the 2022 plot. Neither target was killed.

As for the latest threat, Representative Carson characterized it as a desperate intimidation tactic by Iran. “They’re trying to level the playing field by sending out this threat,” he said, characterizing Iran’s leaders as “losing their grip.”
